input:
This example is concerned with the radiative heat transfer from a hot surface to its surroundings. A blackened plate is maintained at a temperature of 1000 K, and it faces surroundings that are at a considerably lower temperature of 350 K. The emissivity $\varepsilon$ of the plate surface is 0.95, which is quite close to the value for an ideal black body. The net radiative heat flux between two large parallel surfaces can be estimated using the Stefan-Boltzmann relation, which takes the following form:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

where $q$ is the net radiative heat flux, $\varepsilon$ is the emissivity, $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant and the two temperatures are those of the plate and of the surroundings. Taking the value of $\sigma$ as 5.67 x 10-8 W m⁻² K⁻⁴ and substituting all of the values into the expression, the net radiative heat flux $q$ works out at 53.1 kW m⁻², which is a substantial rate of heat loss from the plate. Radiative transfer of this magnitude is of course entirely to be expected at such elevated temperatures, because the radiated flux increases extremely rapidly as the temperature rises, and at temperatures of this order radiation will generally dominate over the other modes of heat transfer unless special steps are taken to suppress it. It should be appreciated that this estimate is based on the idealisation that both surfaces are large and parallel to one another, and the view factors that would apply to the real geometry of an actual installation have not been included in the calculation, so the figure should be regarded as an estimate rather than an exact value.
target:
Calculate the net radiative heat flux $q$ from a blackened plate at 1000 K facing surroundings at 350 K, given the emissivity $\varepsilon$ = 0.95 and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m⁻² K⁻⁴. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; the assumption is stated before the relation because the relation is written for that geometry. For the plate temperature and the surroundings temperature, the net flux is

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

where $q$ denotes the net radiative heat flux, $\varepsilon$ the emissivity of the plate and $\sigma$ the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. The flux is the difference of two fourth-power terms: the plate emits on its own temperature, the surroundings return radiation on theirs, and the net is what the plate loses. Substitution gives $q$ = 53.1 kW m⁻². The fourth power is the check on the result: the plate temperature dominates the difference, and an error in that temperature moves the flux far more than the same error in the surroundings temperature. Radiation at this temperature is the dominant loss from the plate: the flux the relation returns is the quantity a heat balance on the plate has to carry, and an insulation or shielding decision taken from a lower figure would be taken on a loss the plate does not have. The emissivity is the surface property the result stands on, and a surface that oxidises, roughens or cleans itself in service changes the flux by changing that property, at unchanged temperatures. View factors for the real geometry are not included, so the figure is the flux between large parallel surfaces at the stated temperatures; a plate that sees only part of the surroundings, or surroundings at more than one temperature, exchanges less or more than the stated value by the geometry the estimate leaves out.
